title: Olivia Dhein: Lawyers, AI, And The New Non-Negotiable
author: Olivia Dhein · Philip Young

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source offers anecdotal support for the narrower claim that general-purpose LLMs can address legal questions, but it does not assess specialist workflow layers, lawyer–engineer collaboration, human verification, governance or deployment models. It therefore provides too little evidence to determine a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

And it gave me something that was uh even then it was at the level of a trainee.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: The source develops the cluster’s organisational-redesign proposition by identifying captured lawyer decision traces as a potential mechanism for encoding expertise into repeatable systems. It also sharpens the cluster’s qualification that legal judgment cannot be straightforwardly standardised, because capable lawyers may reach opposing conclusions; the claimed review gains remain second-hand and limited to bounded first-level tasks.
qs: and he was saying that he felt that Harvey's moat wasn't just their distribution, the fact that lots of law firms are already using them, but also they captured what he called decision traces.
The challenge there I think though is that in a lot of legal situations, it is just a question of judgment and you could have two equally good lawyers who reach out entirely opposite views on things.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: Dhein accepts selective, task-level augmentation and materially develops it into a capability-matching method: decompose workflows, then use AI according to the demands of each task. She identifies drafting as a strong, prompt-dependent use case while reserving complex legal research beyond current models. Her position is practical rather than empirically measured and does not directly address verification, junior development or staffing leverage.
qs: And depending on what it is, then you can advise whether and how you should use AI to do it.
So even the most advanced reasoning models, they can do some legal research for you, but not that really complicated stuff that city firms get paid to do.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Dhein supports the cluster’s cautious, task-specific approach to delegation: legal workflows should be decomposed and matched to model capabilities rather than assigned wholesale to AI. Her view that complex legal research remains beyond current models reinforces bounded autonomy and continued human responsibility, although she does not directly address agentic orchestration, error propagation or verification bottlenecks.
qs: And depending on what it is, then you can advise whether and how you should use AI to do it.
So even the most advanced reasoning models, they can do some legal research for you, but not that really complicated stuff that city firms get paid to do.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that useful legal AI requires task-specific workflow design rather than undifferentiated prompting, and that legal judgment depends on client context and may resist capture as a single correct answer. Its optimism about future model capabilities is qualified and does not displace these practical constraints.
qs: And depending on what it is, then you can advise whether and how you should use AI to do it.

There's a range of answers and and sometimes part of it is knowing your client, you know, knowing what your client's risk appetite is and what their objectives are and and are there particular things that wouldn't be obvious that that they would want to, you know, either achieve or avoid.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI-era competence requires retaining hands-on legal learning, developing verification skills and keeping lawyers actively involved in AI-assisted work. It qualifies the threat framing by arguing that some routine junior tasks were poor training and that automation may accelerate exposure to more strategic work, but it still calls for selective manual practice and redesigned supervision.
qs: So they have to learn and develop the skill of what do I need to learn and which bit do I do manually the the old-fashioned way to make sure I really get it and which part of it must I do with AI because it is efficient and it makes sense to do so.
You need to learn how the AI will likely do it, how the AI may make a mistake, and how you find that mistake.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Dhein supports the cluster’s emphasis on buyer-driven work reallocation, human verification and governance: clients are using AI for initial legal advice and asking lawyers to check it, while also scrutinising responsible use and confidentiality. The source does not substantively address pricing pressure, staffing succession or end-to-end delivery redesign.
qs: This is just generally in the market is obviously clients will run something through AI, get legal advice from AI and then ask the lawyers to check it.
And I think the main driver is usually we just want to make sure that you're using this in a responsible way and confidentiality is maintained.

st.t: Expert workflows: Legal context becomes product infrastructure
st.an: The source supports the proposition that capturing lawyers’ decision processes could help products reproduce expert approaches, while stressing that this remains conditional and that legitimate disagreement among capable lawyers limits any single model of legal judgment. Its anecdotal review evidence also aligns with the synthesis’s caution that task-specific gains do not establish broad autonomy or transformation.
qs: And I think that if how good lawyers collectively thought could be captured, then yes, you could see why then you could end up with a product that was able to sort of mirror their approaches.
The challenge there I think though is that in a lot of legal situations, it is just a question of judgment and you could have two equally good lawyers who reach out entirely opposite views on things.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Dhein supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI will automate bounded production tasks while preserving the need for client-specific legal judgment, human verification and accountability. Her examples of AI-assisted first drafting, changing junior work and client scrutiny reinforce a copilot model and selective workflow redesign rather than autonomous legal delivery.
qs: Yes, there's a lot more to lawyering than just what is the right answer.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Dhein supports the cluster’s treatment of AI as unavoidable organisational change and, more specifically, its conclusion that training and career design must adapt rather than preserve repetitive junior tasks by default. Her contribution is supportive but narrow and based mainly on personal experience; she does not offer a concrete replacement training pathway or address the cluster’s broader implementation conditions.
qs: I don't think I needed a law degree to be able to do that and it didn't help me negotiate anything or draft better in any way really.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI will substitute for routine legal tasks while complementing, rather than wholly replacing, lawyers. It anticipates more complex junior work and endorses AI-generated first drafts subject to lawyers’ case knowledge and revision, while offering predictions and professional argument rather than measured employment or savings evidence.

You could use it to prepare a first draft and then of course you can go through the draft and revise it as you think appropriate and hopefully save yourself quite a bit of time and hopefully the client some  money.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Dhein endorses selective, skill-dependent deployment: lawyers should distinguish tasks suited to AI from those requiring manual foundations and must understand and verify AI outputs. Her speculation that models may eventually outperform humans qualifies the long-term outlook but does not displace her present human-led, risk-managed approach.
qs: So they have to learn and develop the skill of what do I need to learn and which bit do I do manually the the old-fashioned way to make sure I really get it and which part of it must I do with AI because it is efficient and it makes sense to do so.
You need to learn how the AI will likely do it, how the AI may make a mistake, and how you find that mistake.

kp.k: AI integration becomes a cross-practice professional function
kp.d: Dhein describes her global Baker McKenzie role as selecting applications, developing lawyer workflows, training lawyers and collaborating with risk and privacy specialists. She distinguishes this internal integration work from the firm's applied AI team's customized client workflows. She reports an AI strategy dating to 2016 or 2017 and a public firmwide Copilot rollout, while observing that document-oriented workflow principles transfer between disputes, transactions, tax and real estate.
qs: I think they've had an AI strategy since 2016 or 2017.
And they have the applied AI team which does specific customized AI workflows for clients.
But this role was actually about working with the lawyers inside Baker McKenzie and looking at what should be adopted, how or what lawyers should do with it specifically across the practice groups.
And my role is actually global.

kp.k: Adoption is framed as necessity rather than innovation
kp.d: Dhein argues that responsible AI engagement is non-negotiable for lawyers in 2026, but describes uneven adoption and continued encounters with lawyers who have never used ChatGPT. She says lawyers overweight adoption risks and neglect non-adoption risks. Young separately reports two unnamed large-firm contacts framing AI as business continuation and business survival; these are reported opinions rather than demonstrated competitive outcomes.
qs: if you are a lawyer in 2026, this is kind of a non-negotiable.
but the risk of not using AI is not even in the equation
but I'm still meeting lawyers who've never used chat GPT.
They see it as a business continuation topic.
They said in order to continue to survive as a business um and not to be out competed, they had to integrate AI into as many workflows as was sensible to do so.

kp.k: Junior formation requires manual learning and AI verification
kp.d: Dhein rejects the reported argument that juniors must repeat traditional proofreading-heavy training to avoid becoming lazy or losing attention to detail. She argues that juniors face greater demands: deciding which tasks to learn manually, which to automate, and how to identify AI mistakes, while senior lawyers are themselves still learning. She recommends generally using AI for summarization but learning legal research manually before checking AI-generated research. Young predicts juniors will move toward more strategic and complicated tasks as low-value work disappears.
qs: I don't think I needed a law degree to be able to do that and it didn't help me negotiate anything or draft better in any way really.
So for example, if you are summarizing something, nine times out of 10, I would say probably AI is something you should use.
But if you're doing legal research, I would probably say to a junior, this is the sort of thing you should probably learn to do manually.
You need to learn how the AI will likely do it, how the AI may make a mistake, and how you find that mistake.
junior lawyers will be expected to do a lot more complicated things.

kp.k: Workflow decomposition should follow model capabilities
kp.d: Dhein recommends starting with the lawyer's task and the model's strengths, then selecting the tool. She decomposes workflows into drafting, querying document sets and translation rather than submitting an undifferentiated task. In her assessment, drafting is a strong application, whereas the complicated legal research for which city firms are paid remains beyond even advanced reasoning models. These are practitioner judgments, not benchmark findings.
qs: I start from the model and then I think about the tool
I think about what is the lawyer doing and then I think about what is the model good at
Is this quering a document set? Is there some translation involved?
So even the most advanced reasoning models, they can do some legal research for you, but not that really complicated stuff that city firms get paid to do.
But drafting is right at the other end of the spectrum.

kp.k: Drafting benefits depend on prompting and substantive familiarity
kp.d: Both speakers support AI-assisted first drafts while maintaining that lawyers must know the underlying case or documents. Dhein emphasizes reusable, individualized prompts and word-by-word review as reasons drafting is particularly useful and relatively inspectable. Young suggests time and client-cost savings, but supplies no measured savings. This is a lawyer-in-the-loop drafting recommendation rather than endorsement of unreviewed output.

But with the drafting, it's just the magic is in the prompting because you can get it to write like you would sound
this is the safest use case in a way because you can read literally every single word that comes out.
You could use it to prepare a first draft and then of course you can go through the draft and revise it as you think appropriate

kp.k: Context capacity constrains document-intensive legal applications
kp.d: Young attributes some earlier disappointing results to users overloading context windows or losing earlier material during extended exchanges. He describes larger context windows and sustained attention across their contents as important improvements, while distinguishing these observations from Garfield's architecture. Dhein likewise identifies context capacity as something she has tracked since early 2023 to assess reasoning and understanding. Neither provides a quantitative legal evaluation.
qs: somebody who was new to an LM might try and oneshot some gigantic corpus of information and then find that the LM does a relatively bad job because of course it's not been able to take everything into its context window.
material that was put in at the beginning dropped off the context window.
I've been looking at context windows since early 2023

kp.k: Declining hallucinations could change verification requirements
kp.d: Young predicts hallucinations will never reach 0% but could fall sufficiently below human error that verification eventually becomes unnecessary; this is explicitly a future claim without a demonstrated threshold or timeline. Dhein emphasizes lawyers' present responsibility to check citations and notes that human error has not been measured for the comparison they discuss. She reports a colleague's argument that outputs at 70% versus 85% correctness can require the same checking effort, and tentatively accepts that sufficiently high reliability could change risk allocation.
qs: although the incidence of hallucinations will never drop to 0% because LLMs are a probabilistic system, it's going to drop to the point where the the incidence of them is far lower than the incident of human error.
there'll come a point where even that's not required because these models are superhuman.
everybody always goes on about fake case citations, which is not an AI issue. That's a human issue where the lawyer hasn't checked their work properly.
sometimes it doesn't matter so much if you have an AI product that's 70% correct or 85% correct cuz you still have to take the same amount of time to check it.
I think we've never measured that. So we actually don't know what we would be measuring against

kp.k: Document review may expose human oversight limitations
kp.d: Young recounts Garfield identifying relevant small-print information he had overlooked and speculates that the human reviewer could become the risk rather than the safeguard. Dhein reports conversations about e-discovery metrics and an unnamed password-detection exercise in which AI found items human reviewers missed. Her transcript reports a market standard as 'something like 7' and model results 'between 7 and.9', without naming the metric clearly or supplying a study, sample or methodology; she confines the claimed advantage to junior first-level review, not senior review. Young links these possibilities to reducing omissions caused by inexperienced, siloed disclosure teams.

they'd be working in silos or looking at particular chunks of documents and wouldn't necessarily see the connections

kp.k: Confidentiality protections remain central to professional deployment
kp.d: Dhein recommends enterprise versions with appropriate confidentiality protections for providing legal services and expresses surprise that privilege concerns remain poorly understood. Young argues that basic guidance and relatively inexpensive subscriptions are available. Dhein reports active client inquiries primarily seeking confirmation of responsible use and maintained confidentiality; she also flags potential privilege concerns when clients themselves submit material to AI. These are practitioner recommendations and observations, not determinations of privilege under specified law.

kp.k: Client-generated advice creates verification and pricing tensions
kp.d: Dhein reports a marketwide rise in clients obtaining AI legal advice and asking lawyers to check it. Young argues that expectations of quick, cheap review can leave firms assuming substantial risk without examining all relevant documents or receiving commensurate fees. Dhein notes the reverse cost outcome: poor AI advice can require checking and correction that costs more than advice produced directly. The discussion supplies no prevalence statistics or proposed fee model.

that's something that has gone from zero to everybody's talking about it.
may not even be able to charge a fee that reflects the risk that they're taking on if it transpires to be wrong.
you're checking it and correcting it, which was actually more expensive than if you' just given the advice by itself, just using your own expertise.

kp.k: Future capability expectations draw on cross-domain research
kp.d: Dhein uses reported research on Anthropic's poetry planning, Gemini's rare-language learning within context and model architectures as indicators for potential legal reasoning development. She sees no current limit but explicitly allows that one may emerge. Young speculates that richer multimodal representations will improve outputs and identifies real-time learning as an unresolved question for AGI. Dhein extends this speculation to richer understanding of justice and models observing lawyers at work; none of these possibilities is presented as a demonstrated legal-service outcome.

It's a very long way of saying I don't see a limit at the moment. It doesn't mean we might not find one
more and more models will become multimodal.

kp.k: Decision traces could capture otherwise tacit legal judgment
kp.d: Young reports Harvey co-founder Winston's argument that its competitive moat includes decision traces, not merely distribution: records of lawyers choosing and amending clauses or making litigation decisions. Young suggests these could enable products to mirror lawyers' approaches but stresses that equally competent lawyers may reach opposite conclusions, illustrated by his own successful litigation application against another lawyer's advice. Dhein speculates, by analogy to reported medical-imaging successes, that AI could identify patterns underlying lawyers' intuitions that lawyers cannot articulate. These remain reported commercial claims, anecdote and analogy rather than validated findings about legal judgment.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dhein argues that engagement with AI is already a professional necessity, rather than an optional innovation activity.
pts.d: Speaking about 2026, Olivia Dhein says lawyers cannot avoid AI's effects on their profession. She describes uneven adoption: some firms actively deploy and discuss tools, while others remain publicly quiet or cautious. Her basis is her integration role and conversations with lawyers, including some who have never used ChatGPT. She argues that focusing only on the risks of adoption omits the risks of not adopting. Public silence is presented as an observation, not proof of non-adoption.

pts.k: Dhein describes AI integration as a cross-practice operational activity involving workflow selection, training and risk assessment.
pts.d: Dhein reports that Baker McKenzie has rolled out Copilot and actively considers additional tools. Her global role involves identifying what lawyers should adopt and how they should use it, alongside training and collaboration with risk and privacy specialists. She says document-focused AI principles can transfer between disputes, real estate, M&A and other practices. This is a report of current organisational practice, based on her own work, rather than a measured productivity finding.

pts.k: Dhein predicts a more demanding learning pathway for junior lawyers, not inevitable laziness or loss of legal competence.
pts.d: Dhein rejects the claim that traditional proofreading is indispensable to becoming a good lawyer, drawing on her own trainee experience. She argues that juniors must now decide which tasks to learn manually and which to perform with AI, while senior lawyers are still learning how to guide them. Her examples favour AI for most summarisation but manual learning of legal research, followed by learning how AI conducts research, where it fails and how to verify its output. This concerns skills and training, not a quantified prediction about junior headcount.

pts.k: Dhein identifies drafting as a strong current use case, while saying the most complex City-firm legal research remains beyond current models.
pts.d: Her workflow approach separates drafting, document querying and translation rather than treating all legal tasks alike. She says models draft quickly and can be tailored to a lawyer's style, subject to effective prompting and the lawyer reading the underlying material. She regards visible, word-by-word output as making drafting comparatively amenable to checking. Conversely, she says even advanced reasoning models cannot currently perform the most complicated research for which City firms are paid. These are practice-based capability assessments, without controlled tests or measured time savings.

pts.k: Dhein frames reliance on AI as a question of verification and risk allocation, with possible changes if reliability becomes sufficiently high.
pts.d: Dhein characterises lawyers' reliance on fabricated case citations as a failure to check work. Responding to the discussion of future reliability, she tentatively accepts that a sufficiently high accuracy threshold could change the risk calculation, while stressing that human legal error has not been measured for comparison. She relays a colleague's observation that moving from 70% to 85% correctness may leave checking time unchanged; these are illustrative figures, not reported test results. Her qualified response does not independently establish the host's stronger prediction that hallucinations will cease to matter or that verification will become unnecessary.

pts.k: Dhein reports that AI can already outperform junior human reviewers in some first-level document-review tasks.
pts.d: Her basis is conversations with people in e-discovery, not a named study or independently documented benchmark. She describes established relevance-review metrics, reports a human market standard of approximately 0.7 and model results between approximately 0.7 and 0.9, and interprets this as better performance at junior first-level review, explicitly not senior review. The transcript's rendering of the metric and figures is unclear and should not be treated as a cleanly specified accuracy comparison. She also relays an unnamed cybersecurity exercise in which AI found passwords missed in a parallel human review.

pts.k: Dhein says clients are actively scrutinising firms' AI use and increasingly bringing AI-generated advice to lawyers for verification, which can increase rather than reduce costs.
pts.d: Dhein reports that clients ask which tools are used and seek confirmation of responsible handling and confidentiality. Separately, as a general market observation rather than a Baker-specific claim, she says clients increasingly obtain advice from AI and ask lawyers to check it. Poor output can require enough checking and correction to cost more than obtaining the lawyer's advice directly. She also raises potential privilege concerns about clients' tool choices. No adoption rate, billing data or quantified cost comparison is supplied.

pts.k: Dhein sees no demonstrated ceiling on future legal reasoning capabilities, but makes lawyer-like reasoning conditional on continued model development.
pts.d: She follows reasoning research, context-window expansion and model architectures to assess potential progress. Her examples include Anthropic's work on tracing poetry generation, a Gemini experiment involving a book and a rare language, and her own informal trials of models on legal questions. She uses these as suggestive analogies about rule systems and reasoning, not direct evidence that AI can already perform a lawyer's full role. She explicitly allows that a limit may emerge and that some lawyer activities may remain outside model capabilities. No arrival date is given.

pts.k: Dhein speculates that multimodal AI could deepen understanding of legal concepts and potentially expose patterns in lawyers' judgments that lawyers cannot themselves explain.
pts.d: Dhein suggests that access to more than text might enrich models' understanding of concepts such as justice. She asks whether observing lawyers work could improve models' understanding of legal tasks, rather than asserting an established capability. She also draws an analogy to reports of AI detecting breast cancers that human radiologists cannot see, wondering whether legal judgment contains comparable blind spots. The medical example is unnamed and functions as an analogy, not legal-domain evidence.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The interview relies principally on professional experience, informal model use, industry conversations and research analogies.
pts.d: Dhein's strongest first-hand basis concerns integration work, training, workflow selection and client questions. Her initial impression that a general model answered legal questions at trainee level is an informal personal assessment. The e-discovery figures and password-detection example are second-hand and lack named studies, sample sizes or test conditions. References to reasoning and context-window research motivate future possibilities but do not demonstrate legal-service outcomes. No systematic evidence is supplied for profession-wide adoption, cost savings, training outcomes or a timeline to lawyer-level reasoning.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current claims are situated in 2026; longer-term capabilities are undated and conditional.
pts.d: Dhein contrasts early-2023 experimentation with what she regards as required professional engagement in 2026. Present deployment depends on task suitability, thoughtful iteration, prompting, human checking and appropriate confidentiality protections. Her enterprise-tool recommendation expressly calls for the right protections, rather than documenting a universal guarantee of privilege. Current limitations include complex legal research and senior-level review. Future lawyer-like reasoning, changed reliance thresholds and multimodal understanding are possibilities without a specified deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are large-firm lawyers, juniors, document reviewers, integration and risk teams, and clients.
pts.d: Dhein's concrete examples centre on a global City firm and its disputes, transactional, tax and real-estate practices, although her necessity claim extends to lawyers generally. Juniors face additional learning and verification responsibilities; first-level reviewers face AI capability comparisons; senior lawyers must guide adoption while still developing their own methods. Firms must select tools and govern confidentiality, and clients both scrutinise deployment and generate new checking work by bringing AI advice. The interview does not establish staffing reductions, a new leverage structure, or quantified access-to-justice gains.
